en: Composed by the Tang Dynasty Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhànruán.

In the explanation of the assembly, he first analyzes the sequence. Regarding the phrase "mostly so," there are also instances in the sūtras where Bodhisattvas are listed after [the śrāvakas], each of which has its own symbolic significance. For example, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* does not list the śrāvakas.
Because it is purely [the former] and without admixture.

Most of the older commentators follow Guangzhai; since their views accord with the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there is no separate refutation of them. However, the summary concludes that they appear to represent two distinct interpretations.

The note "and so forth" means that regarding the matter, it resembles the *nidāna* (causal conditions) and must possess the four *siddhi*s; regarding the meaning, it resembles the provisional teachings (*yìjiào*) and must further discuss the eight [aspects].

The matter refers to the person (*shēn*), hence the mention of "intimate and distant"; the meaning refers to the principle of the truths (*dìlǐ*), hence the mention of "Nirvāṇa" and so on. Because their physical forms and dress differ, this corresponds to the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly).
Those who are close give rise to goodness; those who are distant destroy evil; that which is neither close nor distant is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Within the meaning of existence, since there are the three truths, when these truths are correlated with the teachings, the four [teachings] can be discerned. Regarding the four [vehicles], such as the *pitakas*, one may understand their meanings through the four [approaches], such as the gradual.

Furthermore, because the two pairs of meanings both rejoice in *nirvāṇa*, and the four types of bodhisattvas neither rejoice in nor cling to it, they all abide in the middle. Only by reaching the ultimate reality while simultaneously being able to benefit others does one abide in the middle; thus, seeking the fundamental principle therein transcends both the ordinary and the sage.

If one considers those who have entered [the stages] to be bodhisattvas, this refers specifically to the stage of the Ground (bhūmi) in the Separate Teaching (biejiao) and to the beginning and end of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
The commentator says:

"The Śrāvaka’s learning is remote and he concentrates it within; the Bodhisattva’s path is intimate and he forgets it without. This merely grasps the phenomenon while losing the principle; it resembles the trace while remaining deluded regarding the source.
How much more so when considering the contemplation of the mind and its causes and conditions?

Within the context of the "Original" (hon) and the "Traces" (jaku), this sutra’s enumeration of the assembly surpasses that of all other scriptures; thus, the persons who lead—both humans and devas, as well as those of the two vehicles—are fundamentally not of the lower stages. The assembly led by them is capable of receiving both general and specific predictions. Because the words are general while the intent is inclusive, it is said that they are "secret within."
All are Great Sattvas; because they can manifest traces that lead away from the two extremes and distinguish them as neither ordinary nor small, they are called "Sattvas.

Since the term "Bodhisattva" would overlap with their fundamental nature, it is not discussed here; one should know that this [designation] is likewise discussed merely in terms of essence and function.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" following the contemplative interpretation, one should further clarify the contemplation of the various teachings' opening and manifestation, as well as the contemplation of the original and the trace, by means of causes and conditions.
As for the explanation of the listing of the śrāvakas, according to the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, they are listed first for eight reasons:
first, to manifest that those who heard [the teaching] directly will not slander it later;...
2. Because it encompasses those of indeterminate nature who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna;
3. Because it eliminates pride of nobility, as [such pride] is not ultimate;
4. Because one constantly follows the Buddha.
Fifth, because their physical appearance and deportment are identical;
sixth, because they cause their inner retinue to renounce desire;
seventh, because they cause bodhisattvas to show them respect.
Eighth, it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to have faith.

However, among the eight meanings in the *Śāstra*, only the second half of the second meaning belongs exclusively to the present sutra, because those of indeterminate nature attain [the fruit] in this land; yet even this is still incomplete by one half, as those of determinate nature attain it in that land and will attain it in the future.
The remaining seven meanings appear both before and after this section in the *Śāstra* because they apply universally to all sutras.

By incorporating the second meaning into each of the other seven, one ensures that each of the seven individually possesses this second meaning; only then do the eight meanings become fully present in this sutra.
Furthermore, according to our current intention, there are three additional meanings:

because it is intended as a distinct record, because it separately reveals the provisional (upāya), and because it first manifests the fundamental (mūla); thus, these remaining meanings are forever distinguished from the former teachings.
Therefore, the intent of the treatise is that many sutras are similar; thus, it provides a general explanation.
Now, although the various teachings share commonalities yet remain distinct, the Vaipulya (fangdeng) is listed first for four reasons:
because it seeks to supersede [other teachings], because it seeks to guide [beings] subtly, because it causes them to believe in the essence, and because it causes their flavor to transform.
Prajñā also has four [purposes]:
because it desires to cleanse, because it desires to relinquish karmic burdens, because it secretly leads one forward, and because it matures the ghee.
Thus, one should know that the text of the *Śāstra* encompasses the first two flavors; as previously stated, each has its own four aspects, which further differ from those before and after.
The *Śāstra* further states:
There are eight reasons why monks take precedence over nuns:
first, men are honored and women are held in lower esteem;...
Second, the sequence of entering the Way;
third, the differences between teacher and disciple;
fourth, the capacity for transmitting the Dharma.
5. The advancement and retreat of the communal recitation;
6. Whether or not those living together attain [the fruits];
7. The yielding of priority regarding seniority and juniority.
8. Attaining the praise of existence and non-existence.
These eight [aspects] fully pervade the preceding three flavors (*rasa*), yet they mostly pertain to the *dadhi* (curd) teaching.
If one follows the principle that these are likewise Śrāvakas, they still lack the second intention.

Within the current distinction, with the sole exception of the entrustment of the task (*parindanā*), the underlying principle still applies because, as in the case of the bhikṣu, they hear the transmission of the teaching.

Therefore, at the time of the entrustment of the task, it is not entirely without a share [in the dharma]. All other principles are identical to those of the bhikṣu; regarding the gradual teaching within the five flavors, the meaning for the assembly is no different.
Next, the old commentary is cited, which states:

"As for those of great and small renown," the intended meaning is that "renown" refers to one's own name, while "hearing" refers to what others hear; thus, because one is renowned as great, one is heard as great, and because one is renowned as small, one is heard as small.
Now, for the sake of following the text alone, I shall refute their lack of scriptural basis.
To say "following the text" means that one clarifies the extent of what is cognized solely by reference to the number of items enumerated.
The preceding section mentions twelve thousand, further describing them as "well-known to the multitude";

the subsequent section mentions two thousand, yet they are not described as being well-known. Even if one were to interpret "well-known" as referring to fame, the latter passage contains no such mention at all—how could there be anything "minor" about this?

Moreover, as there is no definitive basis for distinguishing between "great" and "small," the initial commentary on the category first provides a general explanation of the five characters, followed by a specific explanation of the four meanings below the section titled "Commentary" (*Śāstra*), because they pertain to the *bhikṣu*.

In the initial general explanation, the five characters comprehensively include all those possessing virtue; since the group to whom they are granted is already designated as "great," how could it merely differ from the lower classes?

Among the bhikṣus, such examples are even more numerous; regarding the four gates, the three liberations, the analysis of essence, the universal wisdom, and the discernment of emptiness—these can only be said to represent his lofty reputation and virtuous conduct, for how could they be discussed in full detail?
Now it is said that he belongs to the same class as those of noble standing.

Next, regarding the separate explanation of the four meanings: first, from "Explanation of the Treatise" (*Śāstra-vyākhyā*) onwards, the character "with" (*yu*) is explained individually; the initial passage provides an explanation by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

If these seven are categorized as the four *siddhāntas*: the time, place, and world correspond to the *yathā-saṃvṛti* (conventional); the precepts correspond to the *puruṣakāra* (benefiting others); the mind and views correspond to the *pratipakṣa* (remedy); and the Path and liberation correspond to the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth).

If we follow the previous three [teachings], then regarding the ancient teachings, the seven meanings consist of only three; the "path," "liberation," and so forth all belong to the sense of "remedy" (pratipakṣa).

In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the seven and the one both belong to the fourfold perfection of the Perfect; although they are distinguished according to the teaching (jiaojue), ultimately they are only the Perfect. Because although there are seven, they are identical, the name "seven" is the "one," and this "one" is precisely the "common" (gong).

The four teachings differ yet are all contained within the five flavors; as this is fully detailed in various sutras, it cannot be described in its entirety here. For now, taking as a standard the praise of virtues according to the Tripitaka Teaching: those who share the same time of being moved by the Buddha, the same location at the Deer Park, the same Prātimokṣa precepts, the same mind of omniscience, the same untainted right view, the same thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the same liberation with remainder, and who are fellow listeners—having already received predictions when the general introduction was recited—are entirely established as people of the Perfect [Teaching] because they possess the seven aspects of the Dharma-body.

Sharing the same wondrous resonance with the response of the Tathāgata, sharing the same vision of the wondrous locus of reliance, sharing the same attainment of ultimate precepts, sharing the same realization of the mind of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), sharing the same unconditioned right view, sharing the same perfected and real factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and sharing the same inconceivable liberation—having received their prediction [of Buddhahood], they are identical to Bodhisattvas; how, then, could one continue to praise their virtues merely as Śrāvakas?
Could it be that the compilers were mistaken or suppressed his virtue?

Therefore, we know that during the period of the four flavors, he transformed according to those flavors; the compilers of the sutras listed him among the śrāvakas from the outset, and thus they praised him based on that original status.

If one does not adhere to the original basis, how can one know that the Śrāvakas possess both provisional and real aspects? Those who are real receive predictions and thus know their source; because the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles was made when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was heard, the doctrinal classification must encompass the beginning and the end. Thus, regarding the three teachings and seven stages, they are either originally three, or they are transformed entries [into the One Vehicle].
First, regarding the three collections (Tripitaka), there is one and seventy-one [teachings], because their arising and ceasing are identical.

Regarding the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), there are two, because they distinguish between the sharp and the dull faculties; since the sharp faculties encompass both the Perfect and the Distinct teachings, it should properly be stated as "three and seven," yet for the sake of generalization, they are collectively explained here as a single category.

Another explanation for why they are called "immeasurable" is that, whether in terms of self-cultivation or transforming others, there are four gates both horizontally and vertically; yet the ways in which one enters through each of these gates via the four *siddhāntas* differ.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the "one" [gate] exists because the initial aspiration and the ultimate consummation are not two distinct things.

The expositor should explain this in detail according to the four teachings, even down to the flavor of the teaching, first making provisional judgments and subsequently revealing their ultimate opening.

The phrase "If not yet... and those following are explained in terms of the fundamental and the trace; they are also discussed in terms of essence and function regarding the fundamental and the trace.

There are no separate Śrāvakas; they are simply referred to as the Tripitaka and the Shared [Teachings]. If the Shared includes the Distinct, it may also be discussed, though this would be an abbreviation.
Furthermore, regarding the two matters of time and place, for the sake of discussing them according to the teachings, it is said that within the Tripitaka, time and place are "merely one";
however, if one follows the original time and place of attaining the Way, or the place where many people gathered together, it is roughly as described in the present text.
Either many persons in many places, or one person in many places, as in the various times and locations mentioned in the *Āgamas*.
Question:
How can there be two kinds of *śrāvakas* at this point?

Answer: This is also explained from the beginning, as detailed in the *Xuánwén* (Text on the Profound), which extensively discusses the various stages of the flavors (*pañcābhisamaya*), such as those difficult to transform and those easy to transform.
Furthermore, there are those who, without passing through the analytical dharma (*dharmapravicaya*), are fundamentally people of broad capacity (*pudgala*), and so forth.
Below the section "Directly Clarifying the Two Meanings," in order to clarify the process of opening and revealing [the truth], we first further distinguish their differences.

Regarding these differences, setting aside for a moment the seven points of agreement, if one further distinguishes them within the seven categories of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, there are three differences and four agreements.
Why is this? The four factors of time, place, and so forth cannot be dissimilar—just as with the assembly, the basis, what is received, and what is realized;
if these three, beginning with the mind, were not distinct, how could they possibly be otherwise?
This is because their cultivation, views, and practices are distinct.

This remains a general observation; it may also be said that the dharma of the precepts is attained individually by each person, and liberation is realized individually by each person. Thus, there are five distinctions and two similarities.

Furthermore, if categorized by person, they could also be both shared and distinct; however, as we are currently explaining the meaning of what is shared, the discussion of the distinct aspects is not appropriate here.

The division of their meanings into three or four categories would merely constitute a digression. Therefore, for now, we shall speak based on the seven commonalities; the similarities and differences regarding the distinct teachings can be understood by analogy.
Next, from "If one arrives" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the revelation.

Regarding the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, it explains that those subject to revelation possess both the provisional and the real; before revelation they possess four [vehicles], but after revelation there is only one. Now, by adding the Buddha-way, this is based on those who have newly entered.

Regarding the four types mentioned in the *Śāstra*, they are: those who are determined, those who are predominant, those who regress from the Great [Vehicle], and those who are through transformation.
The *Śāstra* itself explains:
"The latter two receive predictions, while the former two do not, because their faculties are dull and they are not yet mature."
Furthermore, regarding this assembly, the sūtra states, "conceiving the thought of parinirvāṇa," which refers to their definitive nature.
If they were able to hear it, yet it is not mentioned in the *Śāstra*, how could Vasubandhu have possibly misunderstood the sūtra text?
The Sūtra says:
"And in that land, one shall hear this sūtra. The *Śāstra* merely cites this as a general statement based on what is currently being taught.
Therefore, the Master here simply eliminates those with overweening pride; these are precisely the five thousand who rose and departed.
Although they departed from their seats, they are nonetheless categorized as being within the state of *nirvāṇa*.

Since they were able to hear [the teaching] at the conclusion of the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*), those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) did not fail to hear it either; for they had already heard the brief exposition and were present later on. However, one cannot say that they received a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) in this specific assembly. Because the three stages of planting the seed, ripening, and liberation proceed without interruption from beginning to end, according to the present text, all four types [of practitioners] attain [the result] when viewed from both near and far perspectives.

Now, regarding the term "abiding in the fruit" (sthita-phala), it encompasses both those who are certain [of their attainment] and those who may regress from bodhi; because there is a distinction between abiding in the fruit and its transformation, two teachings are differentiated. Therefore, these two types are collectively established as "abiding in the fruit."
Furthermore, the term "Buddha-way" (buddhamārga) is established according to the meaning of the sutras.
If this is so, then the Buddha-way of response-transformation (nirmāṇakāya) should also have distinct provisional and perfect aspects.
Question:
What is the distinction between a manifested transformation (nirmāṇa) and the Buddha-way? Answer:

The "Responsive Transformation" (nirmāṇakāya) refers to the manifestation of traces and is spoken of in terms of the ancient sages; the "Buddha Path" refers to benefiting others and is spoken of by the new commentators.

Furthermore, the Responsive Transformation is understood from the perspective of the physical body, while the Buddha Path is understood from the perspective of the teaching. Since the Buddha Path involves speech that causes others to act, it is termed "benefiting others"; since the Responsive Transformation carries the sense of initiating [an appearance], it is termed "manifesting traces."

Since they are designated by the name "śrāvaka," in the past they lacked the title of "nirmāṇakāya Buddha," and in the present they lack the designation of "one who abides in the fruit with certainty.
How could there not be nirmāṇakāyas among those of overweening pride?
Is it that the "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) excludes this?

Moreover, since the *Śāstra* definitively states that those with overweening pride (*abhimāna*) are likewise "unripe," it cannot be that overweening pride also constitutes a failure of the faculties (*indriyabhraṃśa*).
He said: "The term 'not yet' means 'no.

When a person has not yet died, they are called 'not dead'; when a seed has not yet sprouted, it is called 'not born. Therefore, both 'arrogance of superiority' (*abhimāna*) and 'certainty' (*niyama*) can be aroused; this is the meaning of certainty."

Furthermore, the citation from the treatise within this section provides an interpretation based on the distinction between the fundamental (ben) and the trace (ji): the manifested transformation (nirmāṇa-kāya) is the fundamental, while the remaining three are the traces.

There is no difference in the way these transformations manifest as the other three; however, the "contemplation of the mind" (guanxin) alone is absent, which corresponds to the single object of the sevenfold [teachings] in the first two teachings, whereas it constitutes the contemplation of the sevenfold [teachings] in the latter two teachings.
Furthermore, "time and place" refers to the objective sphere of the precepts;
"mental vision" refers to impartial observation.
As for the phrase "The meaning of the Śrāvaka is vast," this is a noble person’s non-discursive discourse.

However, those who rely on the teachings speak of "Mahāyāna śrāvakas," which does not constitute a thorough understanding; now, it is said that these are manifestations taught from the perspective of the fundamental [nature], and based on the assembly, they are entirely within the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Regarding the term "Vast and Unfettered" (*hào rán*): within the eight gates of the *Zàng* (Treasury) and *Tōng* (Pervasion), each gate possesses four types; each gate further contains the Buddha-way of response and transformation (*ōng-hua*), whose traces in the preceding teachings are again identical to the aforementioned number. According to the fundamental [teachings], there should also be the stages of the grounds (*di*), the dwellings of the grounds (*zhù-dì*), and the stages of practice and direction (*xíng-xiàng-dì*). Furthermore, those confused by overweening pride (*shàng-mán*) are again identical to the aforementioned number. Others lack explanations concerning the provisional and definitive (*quán-shí*), the opening and closing (*kāi-hé*), and the ancient and modern, or the fundamental and the trace (*běn-jì*), merely speaking of dwelling in the fruit (*zhù-guǒ*) and the stage of skillful means (*fāng-biàn*). Therefore, it is said that those who value [this teaching] do so because it realizes *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it is fully explained as previously analyzed.
To explain "Great" (mahā-), the preceding section used "common" (sādhāraṇa) to explain "with" (sa-).

Ānanda was "with" those twelve thousand; this does not merely mean being with people, but rather being with the seven types of persons. Since all seven among them are "great," it is said "with the Great."
Since this differs from the four previous explanations of the character "with" (與), its great significance must be aligned with them.

Furthermore, while the meaning of the preceding "with" encompassed both time and other factors, the current explanation of the character "great" (大) applies solely to one who possesses the seven qualities, and moreover, encompasses many superior attributes.

Furthermore, the explanation of the character "together" (*saha*) encompasses both the agent and the object; however, the current explanation of the character "great" (*mahat*) refers solely to the object. This follows Ānanda’s designation of another as "great. Herein, the first citation from the treatise is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Dapin*), because at that stage the mind had not yet undergone transformation.
Furthermore, the Master’s current intention also comprises three phrases, because each individual phrase encompasses the three meanings found within the *Śāstra*.

These three meanings comprehensively include the four *siddhāntas*: "Great" corresponds to the worldly (*loka*), "Many" corresponds to the personal (*puruṣakāra*) and the remedial (*pratipakṣa*), and "Supreme" corresponds to the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
One should clearly understand that the three mindfulnesses differ from those of outsiders, as well as the reasons why these three mindfulnesses are more numerous, vast, and superior.
Furthermore, one should apply these three mindfulnesses to the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold teachings), as is fully detailed in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhi guan fu xing chuan hong jue*.
Regarding the "Four Vedas," this is as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Sūtra Commentary* (*Jing shu*) and in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhi guan chao*.

Next, within the section on the classification by teaching (*jiao*), the previous first interpretation is cited and judged to belong to the Tripitaka; because it conforms to the preceding text, it simply mentions "that which is revered" and so forth, as before.

From the passage "Now, 'bright'... onwards, the meaning should be understood as applying to both the partial (Tripiṭaka) and the perfect (Vimalakīrti) teachings; however, because the preceding text provisionally explained it in contrast to the external [teachings], it refers to the "Three Piṭakas.

Next, from the passage "As for 'great'... onwards, it concerns the latter three teachings. Initially, it clarifies the sense of "many," which refers only to phenomena (*dharma*); yet, one cannot further increase the number of these latter three. Rather, "many" is explained in terms of what is known. Therefore, the preceding general explanation establishes that each of the three—Great, Many, and Superior—possesses three meanings, such that each subsequent term is progressively more excellent than the one before.

Regarding the distinction between the Separate and Perfect [vehicles]: formerly, it was from the beginning; now, it is from the attainment of the prediction, thus preserving the path of the teaching as distinct.
As for the term "Arhat of Great Power," this refers to the greatest among Arhats, namely those with the liberation of being free from doubt (*aniyata-vimukti*).

Next, within the section on the Original and the Traced, there are first three parts describing the Original; next, from "The Traced Manifestation" downward, there are three parts describing the Traced:

first, it clarifies the greatness of the Original; second, from "The Original Attainment" downward, it clarifies the superiority of the Original; third, from "Previously Already" downward, it clarifies the multiplicity of the Original.
"Zi-jie" (sighing/contemplating) refers to deliberating on a matter.
One sighs only after having deliberated; it is not done casually.
As for the term "Victorious Banner," this borrows the phrasing from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Regarding the statement "surpassing all non-Buddhists," according to principle it should rather say "surpassing all partial and limited [teachings]. However, although that which is surpassed is proximate, that which surpasses it is remote; thus, it is also logically consistent.

Next, regarding the "trace" (迹), the initial manifestation of craving and views occurs within the "milk flavor"; thus, these five flavors encompass the twelve thousand [teachings], as both the provisional and the real are experienced therein. Now, because we follow the provisional aspect, it is called the "trace."

Regarding the phrase "For a long time" followed by "and so forth," each has its own long-standing basis; according to the length of these bases, the teaching was established in the interim, and today it likewise resides within the various flavors of Śākyamuni Buddha’s dispensation.

In contemplating the mind, one first directly confronts the three [aspects] within the center; subsequently, although these are established based on the center, they fully possess the great, the many, and the superior, and should likewise be established separately for the empty and the provisional, each with its own three.

Regarding the statement "one mind is all minds," both the subjective mind and the objective realm are mind, and each encompasses all things, because nothing exists that does not emerge from the three thousand realms.
This is exactly as stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

If something were not subsumed within the three thousand [realms], it would not be universal; if it were not subsumed by the perfect mind, it would not include the three thousand. Therefore, the three thousand—both in their collective and individual aspects—are all empty, provisional, and middle.

Since this single passage is thus, he follows this principle throughout; therefore, the meaning of the "five flavors" (pañca-rasa) applies universally to both the upper and lower sections, though the text places it here.

Regarding the explanation of the *bhikṣu*, the citation from Master Zhaò appears in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-vyākhyā*; since Kumārajīva and his four disciples were all in the Later Qin, it is referred to as "Qin terminology."
There are four meanings of "Zhao" (Beggar):
first, one who seeks alms for a pure livelihood; second, one who destroys afflictions; third, one who is able to uphold the precepts; and fourth, one who terrifies Māra.
Master Kumārajīva divided these, assigning the first to the beginning and the latter three to the end.
Regarding "possessing the fears of the two Māras," the first two [stages] of the middle period constitute the causes for fear of Māra.

The cited treatise omits the capacity to maintain the precepts; since destroying evil merely refers to destroying afflictions (*kleśa*), it contains only three meanings, though their sequence differs.

Furthermore, because it causes even beginners to inspire fear in Māras and the like, the statement regarding the destruction of evil pertains only to body and speech, and does not mean the cessation of delusions.

Since both [the practice of precepts and the destruction of delusions] occur at the beginning, how could Kumārajīva’s interpretation be undermined? How could the breaking of delusions through the observance of precepts necessarily occur only at the end?

Furthermore, Master Zhaoming merely translated the name as "Name-Containing" (Minghan) without explaining its meaning of "beginning and end"; how then can scholars of today cause the Māras to be terrified?
As for the "five fetters," they are fully explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary.
Regarding the phrase "one field" (*ekakṣetra*) and so forth: "field" refers here to agriculture.
One should say that there are four kinds of laypeople who act in accordance with the Dharma, with the addition of "industry.

In the section beginning with "The Jewel Beam of Nirvāṇa," the meaning of the sūtra is briefly explained; although it does not fully possess the three or four meanings, its fundamental purpose is the destruction of evil.

Now, to clarify that these three meanings should apply to both the beginning and the end: this principle should be understood in terms of the teachings, while also implicitly critiquing Sengzhao and Kumārajīva. It is not merely that the text of the *Śāstra* applies to the later [stages], but it also applies to all the various teachings; moreover, the *Śāstra* does not provide only a single interpretation based on the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

If one establishes the four *siddhāntas* within this context: the taming of Māra corresponds to the worldly (*loka*), the mendicant life to the personal (*pudgala*), the destruction of evil to the remedial (*pratipakṣa*), and the transcendence of the realm to the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "according to the Sūtra-master" and so forth: the meaning necessarily applies to the beginning [of the text], while the certification of faith (*śraddhā*) necessarily follows later. In the previous explanation of the *bhikṣu* (mendicant), "seeking" (*yāc*) was explained as "begging" (*bhikṣu*); this was intended for those of the Tripiṭaka teachings who seek meditative concentration by distancing themselves from perversity and traversing sensory objects, as they were not yet able to realize that objects are themselves principle (*li*).
Therefore, it is only upon reaching the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) that one speaks of seeking the Truth and destroying hindrances, as the principles are equalized.

Regarding the mention of the eight māras and ten māras in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), because the destruction of evil is so profound, the interpretation of "māra" must be understood extensively, as detailed in the eighth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary.

Within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it is not that the eight [stages] and ten [stages] are not refuted; rather, the true reality (shixiang) is taken as primary while the refutation of evil is considered secondary, and the same applies to the terrifying of Māra.
Regarding these bhikṣus within the context of the original and the trace (benji), their depth or shallowness cannot be fathomed; therefore, their specific rank cannot yet be definitively determined.
Regarding "manifesting the traces through the five flavors": if one does not rely on the five flavors, one is not a bhikṣu of this present sutra.
As for "shackles" (zhìgù), the upper character is pronounced zhì; it refers to fetters for the feet.
The character *xià* (下) is pronounced as *gǔ* (古) with the *wò* (沃) rhyme; it refers to hand-shackles.

The Two Truths are like fetters and stocks, while Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) is like the loosening of bonds. Directing the mind toward non-abiding and regarding objects without attachment, one thus does not cling to either object or wisdom and escapes the house of the two deaths. The "Bhikṣu who terrifies Māra" may be understood by analogy with the [standard] explanation.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": since this is the case for the Madhyamaka, the teachings on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the sequential or non-sequential [arrangements] can be seen through their respective doctrines.
As for the term "assembly" (*gaṇa*), it is because of the harmony of twelve thousand dharmas and matters.
If one establishes the four *siddhāntas*, the first is the *loka-siddhānta* because it concerns the harmony of the multitude;
the section beginning with "The Buddha is eternal" is for the sake of others (*pudgala-siddhānta*) because it engenders goodness in beings;
and the section beginning with "The *Śāstra*" is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* because it excludes wicked people.
The phrase "In this context" refers to the primary meaning, as it resides in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the expression "the harmony of things" and so forth, this is because the monastic boundary (*sīmā*), the Dharma, and the community (*saṃgha*) all pertain to the category of "things" (*vastu*).
Regarding "Dharma and harmony," it is as previously stated because of the seven common truths.

Regarding "the ninety persons of the three knowledges" (*tisra-vidyā*), the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* contains a passage identical to this: "Śāriputra asked the Buddha: 'Among the five hundred bhikṣus, how many possess the three knowledges?'"
"How many are liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta)? How many are liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta)?
The Buddha answered as in the text.
Regarding the "Threefold Knowledge" (trividyā), it refers to liberation through the absence of doubt, as fully explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Regarding "pure livelihood" (brahmajīvika), it is as fully explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the "five expedients," these consist of the four foundations of mindfulness and the four roots of goodness; the five cessations are not the methods of correct contemplation.
As for "departing via the patience regarding the dharma of suffering," there are sixteen moments following the supreme mundane dharma; the departure from the first moment is termed "reality."
Regarding the "partial and perfect five flavors," the five flavors do not transcend the partial and the perfect, and the partial and the perfect do not transcend the four teachings.
As for the statement, "Now is precisely the time of equality," it means that at the moment of attaining the assurance of realization, one has already received the prediction of enlightenment.

Regarding the phrase "attracting all sentient beings" followed by "and so forth," this is explained in detail in the *Xuán* (the *Dàoxíng Bōrě Jīng Xuányì*), within the section on the sevenfold Two Truths, where the purport of the teaching is clarified through a meticulous analysis of the five flavors, thereby revealing its specific characteristics.

Next, regarding the passage in the *Guān* [Sūtra] that says, "If it were otherwise," and so forth: because the method of cultivating contemplation is established according to this present sūtra, if one does not rely on the Middle Way as the life-force of contemplative practice, one is called a monk who violates the ten precepts; such a person does not understand the characteristics of the ultimate *pāramitā*. Furthermore, those who merely calculate and measure the discipline of the ten precepts through a single-minded approach are called foolish monks.

Those at the five stages and those with the six faculties are called the *hrī-apatrāpya-saṃgha* (the community of those possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame). Those from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) onward are called the *tattva-saṃgha* (the true community).

One should also add the note "and so forth" (*yathā-vistara*), extensively developing the aspects of contemplation by traversing the two previous truths, the ten precepts, and so on, as well as in relation to the four teachings.

Second, regarding the explanation of the number, the direct citation of the number itself constitutes the causal condition (*nidāna*). Furthermore, within this, one may establish the four *siddhāntas* according to their meaning:
the difference in the number is the worldly sense (*loka-siddhānta*);
the arising of goodness upon hearing the number is the sense for individuals (*pudgala-siddhānta*); [the subsequent items follow].
Breaking through evil to enter the truth can be understood by analogy.

As for those who do not distinguish according to the teachings, since the number of categories remains the same despite the differences in the teachings, there is no divergent interpretation; however, if one generates understanding according to the specific enumeration, then the teachings are indeed distinct.
Question:
Why is it that the number of those listed in the assembly and those who have attained the Way is invariably complete and without omission? Answer:

The *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), in its commentary on the section of five thousand [verses] or more, states: "Whether exceeding or falling short, both are preserved as a 'great number'. Regarding the phrase "originally this" and so forth within the context of the "Original and Traces": [This refers to the fact that] although the original teaching is vast and profound, it is condensed here into a single fascicle; likewise, while the traces are manifold, they are summarized into a single volume. Thus, the term "originally this" signifies that the essence of the Dharma is not diminished despite being abbreviated. Furthermore, because the original teaching is vast and the traces are manifold, the phrase "originally this" indicates that the essence remains unimpaired even when the manifestation is reduced. It is like a great ocean being contained within a single drop, or Mount Sumeru being held by a tiny bird; though the scale is vastly different, the fundamental nature remains unchanged. Therefore, the text says "originally this," meaning that the essence of the Dharma is eternally present and never lost, whether in its original form or its manifested traces. This is why it is stated that the essence is preserved even when the numerical measure is adjusted.
Question:
Generally speaking, all that are called "traces" must first have a "source. How could it be that all twelve thousand [teachings] are merely great expedient means?
If this were so, there would only be that which leads, but nothing that is led.

Answer: In truth, it is indeed so; however, because one wishes to apply the four meanings equally, it is said that they all possess them. Yet, their origins are not the same and must be distinguished.

If one has already entered the stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*), the person who leads them becomes part of the two assemblies of the "initiator" and the "influential. Such a person was clearly originally a bodhisattva. Beyond this, those who have previously resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) are also called bodhisattvas.

Regarding those who originally resided in the Small Vehicle: even those who have never yet resolved their minds toward the Great Vehicle are still called Bodhisattvas; this category includes those who originally resided in the Small, those who retrogressed from the Great, and those who were manifested through transformation. Those who retrogressed from the Great and resided in the Small, after receiving their prediction, are all capable of being among the "co-hearers."
Question:

The number of people receiving the prophecy during the three cycles is not large; those who were not present in the assembly were instructed to preach it on their behalf, and these individuals are not limited by the same constraints as the audience of hearers. Why, then, does this section state that there were twelve thousand?

Answer: Although the actual number [of those receiving predictions] during the three cycles is small, it is like the time when Śāriputra received his prediction; at that moment, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings were all part of that same category.
Therefore, within the three cycles, there are also instances where those who are transformational manifestations and those who are actual practitioners receive their predictions simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said in the *Śāstra*:
“The two types—the regressive and the transformational—are granted predictions. This is precisely its meaning.

For instance, while the assembly of Bodhisattvas lists only eighty thousand, the number of those distinguished by their meritorious qualities and granted predictions is vast; thus we know that the assemblies of both the Great and Small Vehicles are listed as the audience, and they cannot be expected to receive predictions.

Regarding the statement that each of the ten realms within the contemplation of the middle realm (*madhyama-dhātu*) constitutes a single realm, this precisely refers to the wondrous object; the various texts merely employ the contemplating subject as a metaphor for the contemplation itself.
Although the Mountain City [text] takes the aggregates (*skandha*) as the object of contemplation, it likewise does not yet establish the inconceivable realm.
Furthermore, when numbers are brought into principle, the numbers themselves constitute the object; since the object and the contemplation are in mutual relation, both are termed "Dharma-gates.

Moreover, the object is established based on the conventional side, so its number may be provisionally maintained; yet within emptiness, even that number does not exist—how could it possibly be present?
However, one must rely on the provisional to establish the empty; the contemplation is likewise so.
Within the stage of illumination, they are still called Arhats from the beginning, yet by analogy with what follows, they all become great Bodhisattvas.
This refers to those at the stage of the Perfect Teaching within the classification of teachings.

Within this, first, regarding the reversal of names, the meaning corresponds to "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*). Next, one gathers these causes and conditions to establish the Initial Teaching.

Regarding the initial section on causes and conditions, the first part clarifies that there is a reversal of names; in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, both the subject and object are indicated together: "should" (*ying*) refers to the wisdom that responds, and "true" (*zhen*) refers to the principle to which one responds. Because it is a person who responds to the principle with wisdom, they are called "one who responds to the true" (*yingzhen*).

Next, although the *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* (The Sutra of Auspicious Responses) appears to provide two designations, its intended meaning refers to the one who realizes, the true reality that is realized, and the person who realizes the truth; thus it is called a "True Person" (*zhēnrén*), the three meanings of which will be explained below.

Next, regarding the three [sections] within the "No Translation" category: the first explains from the perspective of the fruit; the section beginning with "Or it is said" explains from the perspective of the cause; and the third, beginning with "If one discusses," determines the source of the name.
Regarding the initial mention of "fields for future lives," these fields simply exist; this is explained in detail in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.
As for the "ninety-eight afflictions" (*āśrava*), they consist of the eighty-eight [afflictions] plus ten [afflictions] of the stage of contemplation (*vicāra*).
If one establishes the four *siddhāntas*, the initial clarification of what has a corresponding translation refers to the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly);

among those without a corresponding translation, that which generally concerns causes is the *puruṣa-kāra-siddhānta* (the human-effort), that which follows from conditions is the *pratikāra-siddhānta* (the remedial), and that which follows from the fruit is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate).
In the provisional teachings, the term "not a thief" is used because they still derive their name from the Two Vehicles.
If, even within the Perfect and Distinct Teachings, they are still termed "thieves," then they must be killed.

Regarding "non-arising within arising": this refers to taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as proof and arising outside the realms; because this non-arising is itself arising, one does not allow it to arise.

To provide for what is appropriate for that [state] is called "provisioning. This is like the passage in the *Āgama* where the Buddha went to an araṇya and spoke to the bhikṣus, as fully recorded in the fourth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, one should further distinguish that while the two preceding teachings differ in their ability to "kill" [delusion], the latter two teachings also differ in how they do not "rob" [the true nature].

Regarding the phrase "all praise the virtues of the first stage and the first dwelling": in the former case, the school that employs translations uses "three" as the name; in the subsequent case, the school that does not employ translations takes "three" as the meaning. Since meaning is itself virtue, within these teachings "three" is taken as virtue.

If one follows the entry into the stages, which is not fixed, it should fully be stated as "from the stages and dwellings above, down to those below the Buddha"—that is, praising the fundamental basis according to the Separate and Complete Teachings.

Next, regarding the two layers within the provisional and the real (honji-suijaku), first there is the application of the three meanings of the Small Vehicle, and next there is the application of the three virtues of the Great Vehicle.

In the former, the provisional name is used to express the real and the provisional; in the latter, the real name is used to extend to the provisional. This is because it is intended to clarify that while the names are common, their meanings are distinct.
If one explains this in terms of essence and function: the former explanation clarifies the essence by way of its function, while the latter establishes the function by way of its essence.
Furthermore, the three meanings of the former explanation are common to the past [teachings], whereas the three virtues of the latter explanation pertain exclusively to the present [teaching].

If, in the case of the distant past, both the origin (*hon*) and the trace (*shaku*) are equally traces, then here, as both layers are combined, the name "origin" is established for both the Great and Small Vehicles; because the force of this meaning is inexhaustible, it is annotated with "and so forth" (*un-un*).
Therefore, because the fundamental Great Wisdom of Equality is neither destroyed nor indestructible, it is able to manifest traces through the various teachings while remaining unarisen;
because the fundamental realization of liberation is neither a thief nor non-thieving, it is able to manifest traces as the "slaying of thieves" within the various flavors [of the Dharma];
and because the fundamental attainment of the Dharmakāya is neither responding nor non-responding, it is able to manifest traces as the "Worthy of Offerings."

In the contemplation of the mind, one first explains by directly correlating the three virtues with the three contemplations, as the three virtues, being objects, can be understood through the contemplations. Next, one correlates them with the three meanings within the names of the contemplations through each individual contemplation; thus, each and every contemplation fully possesses the three aspects, such as "slaying the thief" and so forth.
In the previous section on the original and the trace, names were first explained in correspondence [with their meanings], followed by the three virtues;
now, the virtues are first addressed, followed by the three names.
Within this, emptiness is treated first, then the middle; the middle, moreover, is twofold:

First, the three meanings are explained; next, scriptural passages are cited as evidence to point toward the offering and to praise the profound merit of those at the stages of name, contemplation, and practice.
The citations from the Vaipulya texts are provided in full according to the second fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary.
Regarding the phrase "The following text says," etc., the "Dharma Master Chapter" states:
"The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja:

'If there are evil persons who, with unwholesome minds, revile those—whether lay or ordained—who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra, their transgression shall be exceedingly grave,' as detailed in the subsequent text."

The "eight winds" are gain, loss, defamation, praise, renown, insignificance, suffering, and pleasure—four adversities and four favors. Since even the Buddha long ago transcended ignorance regarding these adversities and favors, how much more so for those in the human realm?
Regarding "losing the opportune time," it refers to losing the opportunity for union with the Path when one gives rise to sorrow and suffering.

As for the passage from "great loss" down to "and so forth," the reason for citing both the Vaipulya (fangděng) sūtras and this very sūtra is that these two are identical in terms of the non-arising of names and contemplative practice (*guanxing*); indeed, all textual passages concerning every form of contemplative practice should have been cited here, but they are cited specifically because the stage of contemplative practice is most relevant in this context.

Regarding the citation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* and other texts herein: that treatise analyzes sixteen phrases according to three gates. First is the "Gate of Successive Arising," so called because the subsequent [phrases] explain the preceding ones.
Second, the General-Specific Gate: the single phrase "all are arhats" is termed the general;

the subsequent phrases explain the former and are thus termed specific. Now, first following the *Śāstra* by means of this General-Specific Gate, I shall not employ the various phrases of the *Śāstra* itself, but will instead rely on the five phrases of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the explanation, while further combining those five phrases into the Three Virtues.

Third, regarding the section on the "Inclusion of Matters," the *Śāstra* enumerates sixteen phrases in full to explain the "counter-matters. However, the *Śāstra* text merely uses these sixteen phrases to explain five [of them] without stating that the sūtra is incomplete; therefore, the sixteen phrases are not employed here. Since this section begins with a distinct [treatment], it is thus a general praise based on the teachings of the past.
Regarding the "three outflows" (āsravas): first, the outflow of desire (kāmāsrava), which refers to all afflictions of the desire realm excluding ignorance;
second, the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava), which refers to all afflictions of the two higher realms excluding ignorance;
third, the outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava), which refers to the ignorance of the three realms.

Regarding the citation of two treatises and one vinaya: the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Cheng lun) explains the loss of benefit (*śīla-hāni*) as applying to both cause and fruit; the *Vinaya* focuses exclusively on the cause; and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Pi tan) concerns only the fruit. Because the benefit is lost, both cause and fruit are lost.
The section beginning with "Precisely because" (良由) reiterates the three failures and clarifies their underlying causes.
First, it explains that the failure to attain benefit stems from karmic causes; this is precisely the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

Next, the section beginning with "creating [various]" explains how causes invite effects, namely the suffering of birth and death; "causes" refers to the *Vinaya* texts, while "effects" refers to the *Abhidharma*.

Next, the section beginning with "losing the body" re-explains these three phrases: because of the three aforementioned faults regarding the three virtues, one falls into birth and death; thus, by losing the Dharma-body, one loses the life of wisdom through the creation of karma, and by losing the Path, one forfeits the precious treasure.

The meaning is this: in the sutra, the single phrase "all outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*); because the three characteristics such as "losing the path" and so forth arise from them, they are given the same name, "outflow," and for this reason it is cited here.
What are the characteristics of the outflows (*āsrava*)?

Therefore, from this point downward, there is an extensive analysis of view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought-delusions (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). In each of the subsequent sections, one should likewise observe how the errors of past scholars regarding the interpretation of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) are refuted.
The phrase "afflictions" (*kleśa*) below explains the second line.
While the first line concerns the relative relationship between cause and effect, this line refers exclusively to the causal state.
Regarding the term "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*) and so forth, these latent tendencies are the ninety-eight [defilements].
The "enabling" (nīvaraṇa) acts as the agent, while falling into birth and death constitutes that which is acted upon.

The "flows" (āsrava) are the four flows: namely, desire, existence, views, and ignorance. The "yokes" (ogha) are named identically to the flows. The "fetterings" (paryavasthāna) are the ten fetterings.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), along with regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and lethargy (*styāna*); they are ten when anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are added."
"Coverings" refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
Regarding "attainment" (*prāpta*): "attain" (*prā*) means to reach.
Because it is specifically for the purpose of eliminating delusions, the term "merit" (*guṇa*) is said to "reach" [them].

Regarding the phrase "the merit of wisdom and abandonment": because he previously slew the mara, he has accomplished the merit of abandonment; since abandonment is necessarily accompanied by the function of wisdom, he has perfected his own benefit. Because he has perfected his own benefit, he is worthy of being an object of offerings.

Next, regarding the passage "having exhausted all fetters of existence" (*sarvabhava-saṃyojana-kṣaya*) and so forth: by citing the simultaneous removal of both cause and effect, it clarifies that the mind has attained mastery (*vaśitā*).

Regarding the statement "an Arhat should merely have his fetters exhausted" and so forth: since those who have [merely] exhausted [fetters] are not what is being praised here, it is said that this is merely speaking of the fruit within the context of the cause.

Some say that while the retribution for their existence lasts for twenty-five lifetimes, their end will not be long away; even if they wait for a future Buddha like Kāśyapa, it still cannot be called "long."

If all Arhats sustain this retribution body through the power of ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭi-samādhi*) and enter the transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*), for what reason does the Buddha’s body enter *nirvāṇa*?
If you say that the Buddha’s body is merely a provisional manifestation, which text in that teaching states that it is a provisional manifestation?

If all arhats who encounter the Lotus Sutra turn their minds toward enlightenment without exception, for what reason are the four great arhats and the sixteen arhats excluded, while all others enter parinirvāṇa?
Those who are flesh-and-blood Bodhisattvas who have attained non-arising (*anutpāda*) should all be non-extinguished.

The phrase "mastery of mind" explains the preceding phrase: for those with dual liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), there must be the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); for those with exhaustion of causes, the fruit must cease. Although one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) may regress, they will certainly attain this [liberation] in this very life; since those with both types of liberation necessarily possess wisdom, it is said that they are "fully endowed."
Therefore, afflictions are regarded as thieves and birth-and-death as life; for this reason, the ancients failed to comprehend this principle and thus fell into error.
Thus we know that the five virtues and the three dharmas are in essence one and the same.
The general and specific explanations according to the *Śāstra* are now complete.

Next, if one follows the *Śāstra*’s "ascending sequence" (*uttarottara-prasthāna*) method: the intent of the *Śāstra* is that after the first phrase has been used to explain the phrase "Arhat," it proceeds until the fifth phrase is used to explain the fourth; the remaining phrases are not further explained. Following this principle, each subsequent lower phrase is used in turn to explain the preceding higher one; thus, it is called the "ascending sequence.
Consequently, with respect to the phrase "Arhat," these five phrases also constitute both the general and specific [explanations] as well as the ascending sequence.

In the section on the "Original and the Traces," the first part clarifies that the five phrases [of the Lotus Sutra] represent the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of the Original; the subsequent section beginning with "The Traces are shown" indicates that the five phrases and three virtues of the Two Vehicles are the Traces. Initially, returning to the ancient [teachings], it establishes non-arising as a virtue; thus, the Original abides in the secret treasury to manifest the three virtues of the Arhat. Nirvana is the general term used in contrast to non-arising, corresponding to the first two phrases. The word "afflictions" (*kleśa*) refers to the phrase regarding the exhaustion of afflictions; the words "outflows" (*āsrava*) refer to the phrase regarding the exhaustion of all outflows. The passage beginning with "no longer" explains the aforementioned two phrases, clarifying that being free from the two extremes is precisely the Original non-arising. The section beginning with "Dharma-body" explains the benefit for oneself inherent in the Original. Although the preceding two phrases generally mention nirvana, this section clarifies that nirvana is one's own personal benefit; therefore, it must be described specifically.

Within these two phrases, the former clarifies cultivation and the latter clarifies nature; as cultivation and nature correspond to one another, wisdom and cessation correspond to the Dharma-body, thus cultivating the three virtues.
The two characters "true reality" (*shixiang*) refer to the nature-dharmakāya.
The two characters "merit" (*gongde*) refer to the two virtues of the nature.
Thus, the fundamental benefit and the cultivated nature are fully possessed, demonstrating that even the Two Vehicles possess the three virtues.

The passage beginning with "Attaining kingship" below clarifies the four and five phrases concerning the fundamental and the trace. Following the ancient masters, these are treated as the virtues of slaying the thief: "destroying existence" corresponds to the fourth phrase, and "the nature of self" corresponds to the fifth phrase, because the thieves of affliction have been destroyed.
Regarding the "King Samādhi," the *Xuán* text explains that each of the twenty-five samādhis possesses four meanings:
first, the various faults and afflictions; second, the merits of the fundamental dharma; third, the completion of the practice; and fourth, the destruction of existence through compassion.
The "merits of the original ground" have long been accomplished; these are the three original virtues (*triguṇa*).
"Calamities" refers to the three [factors] beginning with the "thief.
The fulfillment of the three original virtues constitutes the "concluding practice."
When the cost was incurred, it should have been offered as a sacrifice to destroy existence; that we now instead employ the ancient meaning is because there is no great error in doing so.
Thus, one should know that "already exhausted" also implies "non-arising," and the sense of "exhausting the fetters" extends to the destruction of the "thief."

The "Eight Sovereign Powers" (aṣṭavaśitā) are also called the "Eight Divine Transformations," as fully detailed in the *Commentary on the Mohe Zhiguan* and the *Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning*.

With respect to the contemplation of the mind, these also comprise five phrases: the first is the first virtue consisting of two phrases; "the capacity for contemplation" (*nengguan*) is the second virtue consisting of one phrase; and "correct contemplation" (*zhengguan*) is the third virtue consisting of two phrases.
The phrase "although possessing afflictions" (*kleśa*) and so forth reiterates two lines from the third excellence.

The first part explains the initial line; the section beginning with "without severing" explains the subsequent line; the phrase "as if without afflictions" concludes the explanation; and "entering into nirvāṇa" refers to mastery (*vaśitā*).
In terms of names, both the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and its realization are called "nirvana without afflictions.
Within the enumeration of these names, there are first five general sections:

first, the actual number; second, the intent behind establishing the names; third, the intent behind the scriptural evidence for their establishment; fourth, the intent behind the exegesis; and fifth, the intent behind the application of the meanings.

Regarding the frequent citation of the *Āgamas* among the supporting proofs: for instance, in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the names of the four assemblies are listed, each with its own preferences, in order to attract those of a similar kind.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yún yún*) at the end of the "Fourfold Explanation of Each One": it means that the four [categories], such as causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), are no longer listed individually; however, the causal conditions of the various sages are mostly based upon the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-dharma*), because this constitutes the beginning of the response to spiritual resonance (*prati-saṃvid*).

Therefore, the initial causes for all the Noble Ones were originally among the non-Buddhists; yet, in order to refute those outsiders, he appeared among the Śākyas to subdue them, acting as their guide and leader to draw them forth. For this reason, he fully elucidated his entry into the womb, his establishment of practice, and his circle of attendants, teachers, and friends.
Whether acting in opposition or in accord, the transformer and the transformed are capable of mutual influence;

even if there were a beginning and an end such that one reckons them as non-transforming, this would still serve as the basis for later refutation, demonstrating that the traces left by the various sages are not established in vain, for each and every one is nothing other than a response to an invocation.
Therefore, the meanings of the four *siddhāntas* should each be understood accordingly.

Thus, among the hundred bhikṣus listed in that *Ekottarika Āgama*, there were those who established fasts and built merit; those who constructed monasteries and dwellings; those capable of subduing non-Buddhists; those who skillfully provided for the sick; those who traveled about to teach and transform others; those who retired from affairs and remained with hands folded; those fond of wearing fine clothes; those who were shabby on the outside yet lacked shame; those who ate without satiety; and those whose speech was coarse and violent.
Among the nuns, fifty individuals are listed, such as Kuṭāḍanī, who practiced the asceticism of *dhūta*, and Yaśodharā, who subdued the non-Buddhists.

Within the two assemblies of the laity, there were likewise individual preferences; however, regarding the circumstances of these various sages, the current text is brief while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* preserves them in full. Although their specific deeds differ, they are all manifestations of great transformative power (*mahopāya*).

Within the term "Cunda," the initial part refers to the world; "vow" (praṇidhāna) refers to becoming a human being; "practice" (caryā) refers to remediation; and "prince" (kumāra) refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

This ultimate truth remains within the ancient teachings; it is simply that the teachings distinguish between those who advance and those who do not, without fixed location, interpreting them according to specific circumstances to accord with the four *siddhāntas*. This is the case for all subsequent sections as well.

Regarding the phrase "those who previously served fire": although there are many who serve fire, it is not that they first attained the Way through fire nor that fire accomplished their virtue. Therefore, upon first attaining the Way, one receives the names of "illumination" and "incineration. Because the cause—the destruction of darkness—is extinguished, the effect—the extinction of things—vanishes; for though it may not have vanished at first, it must inevitably vanish later, just as when a person falls from a cliff.
Regarding the statement, "Ignorance is precisely the knowledge of non-existence," this is a reversal of the Sanskrit phonology.
That which is known as non-existent is itself the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, it cites the "Ultimate" from among the two truths.

Next, regarding the citation of two sūtras and one treatise: "The ultimate limit" (pūrvakoṭi) refers simply to the true dharma that is to be known. "Vow" is cited from the *Hetuphala-sūtra*, referring to the original vow made when the Buddha was a bodhisattva to save others first; the section beginning with "Furthermore, Kāśyapa" refers to his own personal vow.
The phrase "Now, this great night" below refers to Cunda and his peers.
Birth and death are like the night of the world; because the sun rises, they are awakened.
"Sunlight" refers to the various Great Arhats and Bodhisattvas; thus, both the morning star and the sunlight together shatter the great darkness within their own bodies.
Regarding the phrase "entering the mountains to study the Way" and so forth, the *Rāma Sūtra*, the fifty-sixth sutra of the *Madhyama Āgama*, states:
"The Buddha was at the Mṛgamātṛ Cave and addressed the bhikṣus: 'There are two kinds of seeking: first, noble seeking; second, non-noble seeking.'"
The noble quest is for the peace and security of nirvāṇa.
When I was a youth, at the age of nineteen, I went to Ārāḍa Kālāma and asked him:
"May I practice the holy life according to your teaching?
He replied, "There is nothing that is not permissible."
"How does one personally realize this Dharma?
The Seer replied:
"I have transcended the sphere of consciousness and attained the sphere of nothingness."
Having stayed in a secluded place and attained realization through cultivation, he went again to the seer and described what he had achieved.
The seer asked:
"Have you realized the sphere of nothingness?"
"Have you also attained what I have attained?
Thereupon they led the assembly together.
He further thought to himself:
"This teaching does not lead toward wisdom, nor does it lead toward nirvāṇa; how could one possibly seek a place of further peace through it?
For this reason, he went again to Udraka Rāmaputra and said:
"I wish to train in your teaching."
He replied:
"There is nothing that cannot. He asked:
"Do you know self-realization?
He replied:
"I have transcended the sphere of nothingness and attained the concentration of signlessness; I have long since realized it."
He then practiced and attained it, even leading a community of followers.
He further reflected:
"This dharma does not lead to nirvāṇa."

He immediately went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River at the village of the brahmin Vaira on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where he vowed not to rise until he had attained unsurpassed, peaceful nirvāṇa; thereupon, he achieved the factors of enlightenment and became fully endowed with the four knowledges.
Next, he thought:
"Who should be delivered first?
Having reflected, he considered that it would be appropriate to deliver the two seers first.
A voice from the sky said:
"The two seers have already passed away seven days ago.
I know this myself."
He thought:
"I should now deliver Udraka Rāmaputra.
Then a deity spoke again, saying:
When the second seven-day period finally arrived,
I also knew it myself.
Thereupon, I thought again:
"In the past, these five men attended to me with great toil and hardship.
Having reflected thus, he observed that the five were at Vārāṇasī; having reflected, he proceeded there.
Seeing him from afar, the five men made a mutual agreement among themselves:
"Śramaṇas frequently seek fine food such as polished rice, ghee, honey, and sesame oil to anoint their bodies;
now they have come again. You should simply sit down yourselves and reserve a seat in advance, but do not invite him to sit."
Upon arriving, he said to them, "If you wish to sit, then sit.
The five men broke their established rules; one went among them to seek water, while another prepared a seat.
Once they were seated, he first instructed two people to bring food for three people to eat together;
next, he instructed three people to bring food for two people to eat together.
He then spoke to them: "There are two kinds of practice: first, attachment to the five desires; second, attachment to asceticism. To remain free from these two extremes is called the Middle Way.
Next, he spoke a parable for the sake of the five men, and subsequently taught the Four Noble Truths; the five men attained the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the statement in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* that the Buddha’s departure and stay while preaching the Dharma to three or two people were unequal, it is because the three were his father and the two were his mother; this was intended to demonstrate that the purpose of seeking alms had been fulfilled, and also to show that the preaching of the Dharma was not in vain.

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, when the day is divided into two parts, six people share a meal; when the day is later divided into three parts, five people share a meal, because the Buddha-nature is free from eating at improper times.

At that time, the rule against eating at improper times had not yet been established for the disciples. After three months—some say four months—of teaching and transforming them, the rest is as stated in the treatise.
Regarding the phrase "three paternal uncles," this refers to Aśvajit, Maṇibhadra, and Kauṣṭhila; the others were maternal uncles.

Regarding the phrase "first seeing the signs of the Buddha-way" and so forth: the first sighting occurred with Cunda, serving as a precursor for later people. It should be said that the Buddha is like a drum, the conditions for encounter are like a mallet, and the Wheel of Dharma is like the sound.
Regarding "first hearing": the five people were all at the beginning; because their initial realization was like Chen Ru’s, it is called "first hearing.
"Fragrance" refers to the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga).
In the past, the faculty [of the listener] was like the body, and the Wheel of Dharma was like the fragrance.
The initial awakening is called "donning" (fu); "ambrosia" (ganlu) refers to the principle of cessation.
"Flow of the Dharma" (faliu) refers to the first fruit, and "ascending to truth" (dengzhen) refers to the realization of the truths.
The *Pinfen Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) states:
"The eldest son of the Buddha was Cunda;
the youngest son was Subhadra."
Since they have not yet received transformation, they are not discussed here.

Within the context of the classification of teachings (*yijiao*), one should distinguish the differences between the teachings; however, I shall clarify only the differences in contemplation (*guan*), because it is easier to discern the principles of the teachings by judging them from the perspective of contemplation. Therefore, I shall analyze them in detail according to their contemplations.

Moreover, with the twelve thousand followers headed by Kauṇḍinya, non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the very core of all contemplations; it is intended that by hearing its name, one may recognize its practice and thereby cause others to understand the mind.
Thus, the Great Master praised the ancient commentaries, saying:
"I regret not having seen their countenances; I only regret not having seen those people themselves."
"Now, by seeing their writings, one sees their minds.
In cases such as these, although the person is not seen, their wisdom is revealed.
Since those of the first, the Tripiṭaka Teaching, do not understand that images are empty, the *Āgamas* employ the "blind" as a metaphor.

First, the analogy of the object and cognition is established in general; next, from "the head, etc. downward, the cause and effect of the object are illustrated: just as the body is formed by the combination of six elements, so too is karma formed through combination; karma relies upon the parents just as a form gives rise to its reflection, yet the reflection is necessarily not real—it is because one regards it as real that the subsequent aggregates arise.
Blindness is like the wisdom of non-arising; not seeing is like non-apprehension.
Third, from “If one opens the eyes” onwards, it clarifies arising and non-arising.

Within this, first, because of the apprehension of causes, the fruit arises; next, from “If one closes the eyes” onwards, it is a metaphor for how, due to the non-apprehension of causes, the fruit does not arise. The mirror is an auxiliary cause for obtaining the fruit; furthermore, it is only through the mind’s grasping and taking it as an object that it assists the cause in producing the fruit—the subsequent text follows this principle.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific.
First, the non-arising is indicated in general; next, from "not seeing" onwards, the non-arising of cause and effect is listed in general.
Next, regarding the three sections within the specific [analysis] following "Therefore, the Āgamas... there are two parts:
first, the contemplation of the aggregates (skandha); second, the entrances (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). Within the initial contemplation of the aggregates, there are two [subsections]:
First, the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) is clarified as the object; next, from "If one can... onwards, is the wisdom of the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
This first section further has three parts:
the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*yoga*).

Within the Dharma, the meaning encompasses both general and specific objects. That is to say, based on the calculation that form is pure, the other four [aggregates] are all pure; the same applies to pleasure and so forth.
Thus, the fact that the five aggregates are all pure, permanent, and so on constitutes the general object.

In this context, where "perception" (saṃjñā) and "volitional formations" (saṃskāra) occur, one should say "up to feeling" (vedanā); where "consciousness" (vijñāna) occurs, one should say "up to perception and volitional formations.

The text is presented here in a general manner. Next, the contemplation has three parts: first, the actual explanation of the application of the contemplation; second, from "Once he knows" onwards, the explanation of how the contemplation is perfected and delusions are destroyed; third, from "In this way" onwards, the application of the destruction of causes to the destruction of results.
The initial section also has three parts:
the dharma, the analogy, and the application.

It should be understood that the mirror analogy is not intended for the blind; it can also be applied generally within the Mahāyāna system, as is fully explained in the fifth commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
The first section on the Dharma has two parts:
the explanation and the conclusion.
The explanation has two parts:
First, the individual [analysis];
next, from "Furthermore, it can... onwards, the collective [analysis].
In the passage beginning with "All are impermanent," one should understand that the word "selfless" (*anātman*) is slightly lacking within the discussion of form (*rūpa*).
The section beginning with "This is" concludes [the preceding point].
The section beginning with "Like the blind" provides the analogy;
the section beginning with "This is" provides the application.

Next, from "Having known" onwards, it clarifies how the cultivation of contemplation achieves the destruction of views; herein, the twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) are refuted.
