Next, from "In this way" onwards, the refutation of the existence of phenomena within the fruit follows the same logic as the refutation of the cause, employing the three members of reason: the thesis (*pakṣa*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).
Next, regarding the contemplation of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), first both the bases and elements are presented together as headings, followed by the formal explanation.

Within the explanation, the author first takes this opportunity to clarify dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); thus, one should know that the preceding aggregates (*skandha*) constitute the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) pertaining to the Four Noble Truths.

Within this, first the great ocean is used as a metaphor for the arising of the object; next, from "How so? onwards, the seeds of suffering are used as a metaphor for the non-arising of contemplation.
Regarding the initial section on the object, it first proceeds by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and subsequently applies the analogy of the elements (*dhātu*).

First, regarding the entry [into the twelve bases], it is initially explained in detail by means of the two bases of the eye and visible forms; subsequently, from the section on "ear and nose" onwards, the ten bases are cited as examples.

Within the initial section on the eye and visible forms, the twelve links of dependent origination are fully enumerated; among these, the illustrative text concerning ignorance is found in the *Āgama*.
Regarding the "five blisters," the hands, feet, and head are examples in which the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are lacking.
Next, within the contemplation, there are two parts:
first, the initial entry; second, the application of the analogy of the elements (*dhātu*).
Entering into the [twelve] bases (āyatana) has two parts:
first, the explanation of the eye and form; second, the application of this by way of analogy to the ten bases.
Within the first section on the eye and form, there are three parts:

First, there is a brief clarification of non-arising; second, from "How is it suffering? onwards, there is an explanation by way of arising as a counterpoint; third, from "If one knows" onwards, there is the actual clarification of the application of contemplation.

Within the initial brief contemplation, a foul seed is used as a metaphor for causes and conditions; since craving, anger, and thoughts of desire are taken as the seeds of suffering, the sprout is ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, taking up the dust of good and evil constitutes the "stench and dregs," while the flies and maggots are the [defiled] conduct; because these two do not arise, there are the ten non-arising states.
From "Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya was foremost" onwards is the conclusion, as in the text.
In the contemplation of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), because the object [of perception] and [the subject] are identical, one does not first establish the object.
Furthermore, one begins with the aggregates (skandha), followed by the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
Within the contemplation of the aggregates, there is first a general overview, and following the phrase "Furthermore, contemplate," there is a detailed analysis.

In general, the five [aggregates] are collectively illustrated by the analogy of a mirror-image; specifically, each of the five analogies is used individually to represent one of the five [aggregates], both following the pattern of first presenting the analogy and then applying it to the subject.

Within the initial general section, first the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is addressed, followed by four further examples, which are likewise like seeking a rabbit in a cloth and finding it impossible to obtain.

That both persons and mirrors are said to be illusory is because they each arise from their respective causes and conditions; if even that which is produced by the union of real causes and real conditions is as illusory as a phantom, how much more so that which is produced by illusory causes and conditions? How could it not be illusory?
Just as a cloth or a medicinal herb is real in relation to the name "hare," yet the hare is called an illusion in relation to the cloth or the herb, so it is with reflected images.
How much more so now, when we first perceive that causes and conditions are like illusions—how could the image not be an illusion?
A detailed analysis is exactly as presented in the fifth fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Zhi guan*).
For now, I shall briefly distinguish the specific aspects of contemplation so that they may be understood;

therefore, I will not discuss them extensively. Herein, both types of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are fully present. Following the section on "contemplating the faculties and objects," one contemplates the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). Furthermore, by relying on the elements and bases, the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is clarified; thus, it speaks of "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth.
Within this, there are further two parts:

first, the investigation of the sense faculties, objects, and ignorance; second, from the term "afflictions" onwards, the investigation of the three periods of time as the eleven links, each with its respective metaphor and application.

Regarding the phrase "the village of sense organs and objects" in the initial analogy, the text appears in the twenty-first fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*; it further uses the metaphor of a mechanical device to explain the meaning of the conjunction of the sense organs and their objects.
The Sūtra says:

"Suppose there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket, ordering a man to feed, care for, and watch over them day and night, saying: 'If you cause even one snake to become angry, I shall execute you by the law in the marketplace.'"
Upon hearing this, the man abandoned the chest and fled.
The king then dispatched five caṇḍālas to follow him with drawn swords, while secretly sending one person to feign friendship and say to him:
"You should come back."
The man, lacking faith, entered a village, but he saw no one at all; unable to obtain anything, he sat down on the ground.
Then he heard a voice from the air:
"Tonight, six great thieves shall come."
The man, terrified and alarmed, abandoned it again and departed; eventually, on the road, he encountered a river and crossed its current, and so forth.

[The commentary] concludes: "If a snake harms a person, they do not fall into the evil realms; yet if one lacks the power of the Three Studies, one will inevitably be harmed by the *caṇḍāla* of the five aggregates. If one does not recognize craving as a deceptive friend, one should contemplate the six persons as being like an empty village. The bandits dwell within the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) and the six sense bases (*āyatana*); wishing to abandon them, one must further treat the swift current of afflictions. One should use the boat and raft of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), moving hands and feet, to cross the river of the segmented existence (*bhavāgra*). Even those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) cannot yet avoid it; only the Buddha reaches the ultimate."
The original sutra text used the metaphor of the three vehicles from beginning to end; now, it uses the metaphor of the śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching observing dharmas.

Regarding the term "mechanism" (*jīguān*): "mechanism" (*jī*) refers to the subtle potentiality, in the sense of that which can be activated; "joint" (*guān*) refers to the articulation, moving by means of a person.
Therefore, all binding of body and speech arises from the movement of the mind to form karmic action.
Since it is said that they "gather emptiness," they are fundamentally empty.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (yún yún), the scriptural text is abbreviated; the full details are as explained in the Three Piṭaka Teachings.
For the time being, let it be so; however, if one were to practice contemplation in detail, it could not be understood through this alone.
Next, within the specific contemplations, the object and wisdom are first illustrated by means of a simile; the section beginning with "If one wishes" initiates the actual practice.

At the beginning, the object (*ālambana*) and the cognition (*jñāna*) are first established; next, from the word "blue" (*nīla*) onwards, the nature and magnitude of the object are clarified; thirdly, from the phrase "all of which" (*sarvam etat*) onwards, the intended meaning is concluded.
Within the initial establishment, the object is presented first, followed by the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the initial statement in the section on "Objects" that "the mirror is a metaphor for the Dharma-realm," this refers generally to how both delusion and enlightenment, as well as the beginning and end of phenomena and principle, and self and others, all equally rely upon the single Dharma-realm.
Since True Suchness, while in a state of delusion, can give rise to the nine realms, and the Buddha in fruition is designated as the Buddha-Dharma-realm, they are collectively referred to as ten.

Therefore, the ignorance that obscures the principle for the sake of individual beings serves as the cause for the nine realms; thus, in the subsequent text, both self-cultivation and the transformation of others must involve the severance of these nine. Only when these nine are exhausted can one be said to be fully endowed with the conditions and the wisdom; being thus complete, the primary cause (the true nature) is finally and thoroughly manifested.

Regarding the next point, the measurement of the essence: herein, the eight phenomena such as blue and so forth are used as metaphors for the ten realms. Whether they are treated separately or combined is stated according to convenience; thus, the two vehicles along with humans and devas are combined, while the asuras are further abbreviated and the bodhisattvas are expanded. Furthermore, the first stage may be taken as the Buddha-dharma realm. The various texts’ expansions and contractions should be understood accordingly based on their respective meanings.

Furthermore, regarding "blue," "yellow," and so forth, since the initial mind of a distinct person (pudgala) is no different from that of the [Hīnayāna] Pitaka, one may borrow the analogies from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, with the addition of "long," "short," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "all within the mirror," this does not transcend the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The Dharma-realm does not transcend delusion and awakening; delusion and awakening do not transcend the mind.

Next, there are five further stages of practice, the first of which demonstrates the scope of one's own cultivation and the transformation of others. This is because, within the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*), the nine degrees of insubstantial merit are absent, and thus self and other are severed; one separately cultivates the conditions and causes (*pratyaya* and *hetu*) to adorn the primordially existing, eternal Dharmakāya.

Next, the section beginning with "relying upon" concerns the arising of practice based on the object; it also indicates that the principle alone serves as the basis for being covered by the nine realms. The dharma-realm is simply the dharma-nature, and it is furthermore the basis for both delusion and enlightenment.

Within this context, it should likewise be stated that "all dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding. Ignorance obscures the principle; both the obscuring agent and the obscured object are termed "non-abiding. However, the distinctions among the teachings arise from whether these are identical or different. Now, turning away from delusion to achieve awakening, one focuses exclusively on the rational nature (li-xing) to break through the nine realms.
3. From "Successive" (*anupūrva*) onwards, the extinction of the cause is clarified.
4. From "If there were not" (*yadi na syāt*) onwards, the extinction of the fruit is clarified.

5. From "Arising also" (*utpādo ’pi*) onwards, the conclusion summarizes that both cause and fruit are non-arising; this refers to the non-arising of the two types of arising—within and beyond the realms—and thus they are both non-arising.
The divergent explanations regarding the transformation of beings are omitted from this text as they are not discussed here.
Next, regarding the "Complete Contemplation" (yuan-guan), there is first the analogy and then the application.
Within the analogy, the phrase "contemplating the mirror" refers to the single Dharma-realm (eka-dharmadhātu).
"Roundedness" refers to the principle, the object, and wisdom.
Contemplation is wisdom, while roundedness is the object.
Following this, the section beginning with "non-contemplation" clarifies the characteristics of contemplation.
The "back" is ignorance; the "face" is the clarity of wisdom.
The "mirror" is the cause of the ten realms; the "form" is the condition of the ten realms; the "image" is the fruit of the ten realms.

Furthermore, the luminous nature of the mirror possesses the ten realms, and the manifested images cultivate the ten realms; thus, both the forms and images and the cultivated nature are fully endowed with the ten realms. Neither of these transcends the mirror of the principle of *dharmatā*. Seeing that the luminosity, forms, images, cultivation, and nature are fundamentally suchness, one departs from the discriminative thoughts and conceptions of the three teachings regarding the internal and external of the mirror. By means of non-dual, non-discriminative wisdom, one universally dissolves the mind and its objects, as well as light and darkness, in accordance with this principle; hence it is said, "one does not contemplate."
Since the observed object is not distinct and principle is without clarity or obscurity, it is said that "it is not averse" and so forth.
Since this is spoken in terms of what is attained through cultivation, it is said that "one does not grasp" and so forth.

Next, in the concluding section following "merely observing," the characteristics of the contemplation are presented in general and abbreviated form: it is a spontaneous illumination that observes only the perfect sphere; because it has no beginning or end, it has no boundaries. It is without beginning because it is primordially present, and without end because it is eternally abiding.
"Light and darkness are as before;
there being neither identity nor difference" means that it is neither the image nor the non-image.
"Not grasping" and below constitute the synthesis.
"Initially not grasping" means to dissolve the aforementioned ten realms.
"Good and evil" refers to the six realms.

Because these six are contrasted with the Small Vehicle, they are termed "deviant and correct"; because the applications of the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are contrasted with the Small Vehicle, they are termed "great and small. Since all are entirely dissolved, they are all said to be "non-existent," and one no longer discriminates between what is innate or what is cultivated.

"Only by means of conditions" below dissolves the preceding subject-object mind; for the reality-mark of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is itself the three truths and the three contemplations, which constitute the great bulk of all Buddha-dharmas. Whether dissolving or illuminating, there is nothing that is not the dharma-nature; yet because the essence of the dharma-nature is free from both dissolution and illumination, the entirety of dissolution and illumination is precisely it.
Below the section "Contemplating Afflictions," it is clarified that contemplating the essence consists solely in contemplating the three paths.
Birth is the path of suffering.
These three paths are themselves the three virtues.

Within this, the first part provides a general explanation of establishing contemplation; from the passage "The aggregates, bases, and elements are themselves the Dharma-body" onwards, it teaches the application of the method of contemplation.

The fundamental contemplation of principle does not involve contemplating defilement to eliminate it, for the essence of defilement is inherently void, and its primordial voidness is termed "extinction. Therefore, the wondrous essence being extinguished does not establish the name of "elimination. Since the essence of the hindrances is itself virtue, there is no need to transform or remove them; thus, it is said that birth is itself non-birth.
Next, the passage beginning with "liberation is itself karma" concludes the non-arising [of phenomena].
Next, the section beginning with "these three" provides a further detailed summary.

Next, regarding the phrase "how much more so for the transformative rebirth" (*pariṇāmanī-kāya*), this uses the heavy to illustrate the light: if even the heavy obstacles within the realm [of desire] are themselves Wondrous Virtue (*Mañjuśrī*), how much more so the light [obstacles] outside the realm?
For now, this is discussed in terms of the three paths below; were it to be treated exhaustively, it should be discussed in terms of all sets of three dharmas.

Herein, the perfect contemplation differs from the distinct teachings of the Tripitaka in that it does not first take the object and then the contemplation; whether in terms of dharmas or metaphors, they are non-dual, though the phrasing may appear similar because the objects of contemplation are distinct.
The reason why the teaching regarding Śāriputra’s conversion is explained in terms of its broad meaning by focusing on the aspect of contemplation (*guan*) is because it is the very first.

From the passage "If one hears the letter A, one understands all meanings" onwards, although the various sages differ according to their specific circumstances, when their contemplative practice (*guanxing*) is discussed, it does not go beyond non-arising (*anutpāda*). Whether it be the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) of shaking off defilements or even the secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*), how could these ever depart from the wisdom and severance of non-arising?
Therefore, the subsequent passages can be understood by analogy with this.

The phrase "and so forth" (yún yún) indicates that one must fully include the ten vehicles, the ten objects, as well as the preparatory practices (*upāya*) and so on; it refers entirely to the text of the *Mohe Zhiguan* as a whole.
Therefore, in the "Universal Destruction" section of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, non-arising is likewise established as the primary principle; thus, I shall now briefly indicate its general outline.

If one is not deluded regarding the provisional and the real, the beginning and the end of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and desires to use perfect contemplation to dissolve the five Buddhas’ three cycles of teaching—both in their original and manifested forms—as well as the propagation of this sutra, such that all is none other than the great essence of non-arising, then one will be able to simultaneously recognize the contemplative objects of the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teaching. Therefore, beneath each name, I shall briefly point out its essential direction.
If even when worldly people establish names for their children there is something intended to be expressed, how much more so must it be for the various sages—how could they do so in vain?

If this were not the case, then the name "Unborn" would be established in vain, and the principle of the Unborn would never be realized; the Great and Small vehicles would be confused, and the provisional and the real would remain obscure. This being so, other cases should be understood accordingly.

In the section on the Original and the Traced, the first part establishes the original and the traced by means of the five flavors; here, the letter "A" reveals its pervasiveness throughout the eight teachings.
Next, from the words "sentient beings" onwards, there is an exhortation for all things to emulate this model, whereby the work of the five periods is completed.
Next, from "Not Original" onwards, the exposition of the inconceivable essence and function is completed.

From "Therefore, the following passage" onwards, citations are introduced to verify the revelation of the traces; various expressions therein likewise do not transcend the five periods and eight teachings.
Furthermore, according to their original length, how many times does this process occur?
It is shown that there are five periods and eight teachings leading up to the manifestation of non-arising.

As for the citations from the *Āgamas*, these cite the traces (*traces*) to certify the fundamental [ground]. Within the traces, the fundamental and the trace are used to demonstrate their relative dignity; however, the heights and depths of the original ground cannot be fully comprehended through this alone.
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 31: "The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. It was a dark night with light rain, and the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
'Cover the lamp with a canopy and follow behind me.'"
Ānanda received the instruction and went to a certain place; there, the World-Honored One smiled.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"It is not without cause that you now hold a parasol and follow me. I see the Brahma King holding a parasol and lamp following behind Cunda; Śakra holds a parasol and lamp following behind Kāśyapa; and even Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, holds a parasol and lamp following behind Kapphiṇa."

The reason why this [formula] is applied throughout the general introduction, extending even to the noble disciples who possess the fourfold explanation, is as follows: "Thus" (evam) refers generally to the entire section; "I heard" (śrutam mayā) indicates that one has heard this entire section. As for the time, place, and the Teacher, they necessarily do not vary; these are all the general outlines of this sutra. Furthermore, whether the disciples are great or small, manifest or obscure, leaders or companions, taciturn or eloquent, yielding or assertive, weary of the external and delighting in the internal, turning away from the Great Vehicle and heading toward the Small, or leading those of the Small Vehicle into the Great Assembly to ultimately return to the Perfect—whether it concerns their own causes or fruits, acting as the seeds, ripening, or liberation for sentient beings to provide benefit across the past, future, and present—their experiences are numerous and the times and places are not uniform. This is truly because the karmic conditions of sentient beings have reached different stages of maturity.

Now that we have all gathered here, looking back from the past to the present, we shall ensure that the current teaching achieves excellence both in its doctrine and its practitioners. Therefore, by employing the four methods of interpretation (*catasraḥ vyākhyāyuktayaḥ*), we clarify the relationship between the capacities of sentient beings and the Buddha’s response. From the external to the internal, one subsequently enters the two gates of *dharmatā* (the Dharma) and *paurāṇa* (the Trace), attaining realization through their respective sequences. All of this relies upon guidance, influence, and inspiration; thus, upon hearing even a single phrase—whether concerning a person or a dharma—all becomes a ritual of transformation and can be taken as an object of contemplation. Consequently, for a single individual, it is necessary to employ all these interpretations. How much more so for those of future generations, who must hear the name and initiate practice, receive the teaching and recognize the essence, contemplate the Trace and behold the Origin, and investigate these causes and conditions to illuminate the beginning and the end in their entirety.

If one attains this insight, then regarding a single person or a single phrase of a sutra, one can take it as the supreme object of seeking; one can recognize the capacities of those to be transformed below; one can understand the methods of the Sages’ transformation; one can comprehend how ordinary beings receive benefit; one can discern the similarities and differences in names and meanings; one can know that the principles of practice and wisdom differ; one can know that contemplation is accomplished according to what is heard; one can understand that the traces [of teaching] originate from the fundamental person and dharma; one can believe that the work of transformation is long-lasting; one can look up to the Sages’ grace as difficult to repay; one can know that sentient beings are difficult to transform; and one can know that realizing the ultimate principle is exceedingly difficult.
Those who do not see this regard it as mere profusion; how much less could they grasp its present meaning?

Whenever one hears of any dharma, any event, any person, or any practice within the various sutras, one immediately understands the Buddha-works of the ten directions and the three periods of time—excepting only the Pure Land and the subtle manifestations of transformation elsewhere—and this is even more so when a bhikṣu contemplates it with such intent.

Therefore, one should know that although the lands, Buddhas, teachings, and manifestations of their bodies differ across various realms, the principle of the gates of reflection and cultivation remains no different.
*Fahua Wenju Ji*, Fascicle 1b.
